title: A small clinical dataset tests machine-learning infection classification
summary: In 25 emergency patients selected for suspected severe limb infection and ultrasound-detected fascial fluid, a six-feature random forest reported apparent sensitivity of 90.4% and specificity of 92.2% for necrotizing infection versus cellulitis. These small-cohort estimates do not establish performance for general soft-tissue infections.

source_review.scope: Primary article full-text bibliographic metadata and relevant computational evaluation Methods/Results: sec2.3, sec3.4. Primary-source caveat and denominator review; candidate-panel identity corrected where relevant.

evidence.ai_role: Random forest fitted the represented classification or candidate-selection model; preprocessing and expert reference labels are distinguished from the learned contribution.
evidence.tested: Thirteen infection cases and twelve cellulitis controls contributed the dataset. Four algorithms were evaluated over ten random 80/20 splits; six features were selected using random-forest Gini importance.
evidence.unknown: Initial significance screening and later feature selection are not shown to be nested inside held-out evaluation. Each nominal test split contains about five patients; repeated splits are not independent cohorts. No prospective utility, separate-team replication or causal mechanism is established. This was a selected fluid-positive cohort with different diagnostic ascertainment for infection cases and cellulitis controls, including pathology for the former. The six-feature table does not independently establish a new held-out evaluation after feature selection.
